title: How do you use the 3Cs to get started on an open case question?
description: The 3Cs for case interviews. A quick strategic scan when you need a starting structure for an open question. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: Use the 3Cs by asking three short questions about customers, the company and competitors, then turning the answers into specific things you can measure. It is a quick way to get your bearings on an open problem, not a final structure.
body:
When it helps

The 3Cs, popularised by the Japanese strategist Kenichi Ohmae, is a quick strategic scan. Use it when a prompt is open ("What should the client do about X?") and you need a sensible first view before building a sharper structure. It also works as a fallback set of buckets when you are asked to brainstorm.

The checklist

Customers

  • Who they are
  • What they need
  • How they buy

Company

  • Strengths and gaps
  • Costs and capacity
  • Brand

Competitors

  • Who they are
  • Their share and recent moves
  • Their advantages

An example: a second bakery

A family-run bakery asks whether to open a second shop. Customers: who buys today, and is there a similar crowd near the new site? Company: can the owners run two shops, and can one kitchen supply both? Competitors: who already sells bread and cakes nearby, and how good are they? Three short questions, and you have a first view and a list of things to check.

Turn the Cs into things you can measure

The 3Cs generate possible explanations. They do not tell you which one is true. Take a local gym that is losing members:

  • Customers: are people leaving because of price, class times or crowding?
  • Company: has the gym cut instructors, raised fees or skimped on maintenance?
  • Competitors: has a low-cost chain opened nearby?

Now replace the scan with an equation: closing members = opening members + new joins − cancellations. Suppose, in illustrative numbers, the gym started the year with 5,000 members. Last year it signed 1,500 and lost 1,500, so it stayed flat. This year cancellations were again 1,500, but joins halved to 750 after a rival opened. Closing members: 5,000 + 750 − 1,500 = 4,250, down 15%.

The problem is winning new members, not keeping old ones. That points to the competitor branch and away from a chain-wide retention discount.

How it sounds in an interview

"To get my bearings, I'd look at three things: the customers, the company itself and the competition. I'll start with customers, since everything depends on whether there is demand. Could I see joins and cancellations by month?"

The weak version recites "customers, company, competitors" and stops. The strong one turns each C into a question and asks for the data that answers it.

Common mistakes

  • Using the 3Cs as the whole structure for a case that needs numbers, such as a profitability case.
  • Listing facts under each C without saying what they mean for the decision.
  • Forgetting that "company" includes costs and capacity, not just brand.

Practise it

1. A regional airline's bookings on one route fell 20%. Give a 3Cs scan in three sentences.

Show the answer

Customers: has demand on the route fallen, for example fewer business travellers, or has the mix changed? Company: did we change fares, timings or frequency, or have delays risen? Competitors: has a rival added flights or cut fares, or has a train or road option improved? Then ask for bookings by month and fare type, alongside competitor schedules.

2. When should you move on from the 3Cs?

Show the answer

As soon as you know which C matters. Then build a measurable driver tree for it, such as change in members = joins − cancellations, or profit = revenue − costs.

Where to practise next

Learn which framework fits which case, then try a full case such as FreshMart, where a regional grocer faces a new discounter.
